issues.legal_issue: A trader who accounts on a cash basis receives income when a money-convertible commercial asset is received in satisfaction of a debt, even if the asset is not yet sold for cash.
material_facts: The taxpayer carried on a money-lending business and maintained its accounts on a cash basis.
After a decree established the debtor’s liability, bonds issued by the government were transferred to the taxpayer in satisfaction of part of that liability under a statutory process.
The bonds replaced the debtor’s liability with the government’s payment obligation and were convertible into money.
The taxpayer treated part of the bonds’ face value as principal and part as accrued interest, but did not report the interest in the year the bonds were received.
issues.conclusion: The income embedded in the bonds was received when the taxpayer obtained them, not when they were later sold; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the accounting method determines whether income is assessed on receipt or accrual. For a taxpayer accounting on a cash basis, receipt of money or money’s worth is decisive. Income embedded in a commercial asset received in satisfaction of an obligation is received once title to the asset is complete, whether the asset is accepted by agreement or by operation of law. The Court relied on Californian Copper Syndicate (Limited and Reduced) v. Harris (Surveyor of Taxes), 5 T.C. 159, and distinguished Cross (H.M. Inspector of Taxes) v. London and Provincial Trust Ltd., 21 T.C. 705, because the bonds replaced the debtor’s liability with an independent government obligation rather than merely postponing payment under the debtor’s promise.

issues.definition: When a cash-basis trader in an income tax assessment receives complete title to a money-convertible asset that satisfies a debt and replaces the debtor’s liability with an independent obligation, the income embedded in that asset is treated as received at that time.

issues.legal_issue: Income represented by a non-cash asset received in satisfaction of a debt is measured by the asset’s market value when received, rather than its face value or its later sale proceeds.
material_facts: The taxpayer received bonds payable in instalments in satisfaction of the debtor’s liability.
The tax authorities assessed the difference between the bonds’ face value and the principal debt as income.
The taxpayer later sold the bonds for less than their face value.
The Department accepted that the taxable income was limited to the difference between the principal debt and the bonds’ market value when received.
issues.conclusion: Only the excess of the bonds’ market value at receipt over the principal debt was taxable; the face-value difference was not the proper measure. The Department was to make the necessary adjustment.
issues.legal_principle: Income received as money’s worth is measured by the value of the asset when received. Applying sections 4 and 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the Court held that for a cash-basis taxpayer the relevant receipt occurred when the asset was received, but only the income represented by the excess of its market value at that time over the principal due was taxable. The Court’s approach is consistent with Californian Copper Syndicate (Limited and Reduced) v. Harris (Surveyor of Taxes), 5 T.C. 159; Cross (H.M. Inspector of Taxes) v. London and Provincial Trust Ltd., 21 T.C. 705, was distinguished.
